newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: MINING -- Argentine foothold for Lonrho.
newsitem.headline: MINING -- Argentine foothold for Lonrho.

text.p: British mining group Lonrho Plc has taken a small foothold in southern Argentina and is set to start exploring at an abandoned mine site in the next few weeks, the firm's local partner said.

Lonrho geologists and geophysicists will arrive here soon and start work next month at the Mina Angela site owned by Cerro Castillo SA, Miguel Aclan, the Argentine firm's director and executive vice-president, told Reuters in an interview.
Cerro Castillo's polymetallic operations in the Patagonian province of Chubut were closed down on October 31, 1992.
Falling metal prices and rising local costs made the mine uneconomic to Cerro Castillo's owners, petrochemical firm Industrias Petroquimicas Argentinas SA (Ipako).

But Argentina's long-neglected mining sector is now being swept by international interest. Over 60 international firms have rushed into South America's second-largest country since the government of President Carlos Menem cut away restrictions and pushed provinces into reducing royalties.

Under an agreement reached in June, Ipako sold 30 percent of shares in Cerro Castillo SA to Lonrho for $300,000 and gave the firm an option to buy an additional 21 percent for $1.25 million. The option date was February 28, 1997.

The amount Lonrho must invest in exploration in all the areas in which Cerro Castillo has covered with mineral rights in the province of Chubut is "still not clearly defined but will probably be over $1 million", Aclan said.
"The main attraction is to find more polymetallic and gold mineralization," he said.

Cerro Castillo's polymetallic Mina Angela was an underground operation at about 1,300 meters (4,300 feet) above sea level. The winters are long and hard, so Lonrho's team will need to work fast through the short Patagonian summer.
Mina Angela produced two types of concentrate, one containing most of the mine's lead, copper, gold and silver output. The other contained most of the zinc.

The mine produced 400 tonnes of ore a day, getting 5,000 tonnes of lead concentrates a year and 8,000 tonnes of zinc concentrates. The lead concentrate was 40-45 percent lead, and also included 8-10 percent copper, Anclan said.
Both concentrates were sold normally to European buyers.
Most of the mine's income came from zinc and gold, then lead, copper and silver.
Lonrho's $1.8-billion mining sector includes coal and platinum activities in South Africa and a 37-percent stake in Ghana's Ashanti Goldfields.
